India's hosting follows its successful 2022 summit in Johannesburg and reflects its growing influence. Key attendees include President Lula, President Putin, President Xi, President Ramaphosa, and Prime Minister Modi, who will discuss trade, technology, and climate initiatives. The Indian government welcomed the summit, emphasizing its role in strengthening multilateralism and boosting the national economy. Officials said the event will showcase India's infrastructure and digital capabilities. The summit is expected to set agendas on global governance, debt relief, and sustainable development, with outcomes to be announced in the coming weeks.

Official responses highlighted the importance of the declaration for regional stability. Modi stated that BRICS aims to promote peace without targeting any nation, while Chinese officials reiterated the need for dialogue. The declaration sets the stage for future BRICS discussions on Middle East policy and could influence diplomatic engagements in the coming months.

items.headline: PhD Student Detects Mysterious Cosmic Signal
items.summary: A 24‑year‑old PhD candidate at the Indian Institute of Astrophysics reported a previously unknown radio signal originating from the direction of the constellation Cygnus on March 12, 2026. The signal, lasting 12 seconds, exhibited a repeating pattern not matching known pulsars or fast radio bursts. Independent analysis by the National Radio Astronomy Observatory confirmed the signal's extraterrestrial origin. Preliminary spectral analysis suggests a narrowband emission at 1.42 GHz, a frequency associated with hydrogen line. The discovery follows a decade of increasing sensitivity in the MeerKAT and FAST telescopes. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has issued a statement acknowledging the find and will coordinate with international partners for follow‑up observations. Scientists anticipate that the signal could provide insights into early universe phenomena. A joint observation campaign is slated for April 2026.

items.summary: On March 12, 2024, chief economists from the IMF, World Bank, OECD, and other leading institutions released a joint outlook at the World Economic Forum in Davos, warning that the global economy will face a bumpy year ahead. The economists cited persistent inflation, supply‑chain bottlenecks, rising energy costs, and geopolitical tensions as key risks. They projected global GDP growth to slow to 2.5% in 2024, with advanced economies potentially slipping into recession. Debt levels and fiscal constraints were highlighted as additional vulnerabilities, while climate‑related disruptions were expected to further strain markets. Central banks are likely to keep rates high into 2025, and governments may need to balance stimulus with debt sustainability. The WEF will track developments, and the IMF's forthcoming World Economic Outlook will provide updated data. Businesses should prepare for higher input costs and supply‑chain adjustments, while investors may adopt a more cautious stance. Analysts suggest that firms with flexible cost structures may weather the turbulence better.

The government has pledged to ensure transparency and has invited independent observers to monitor the process. If the petitions are upheld, it could delay the deployment of DSC teams across the state, affecting the projected employment of thousands of young applicants.

items.headline: Supreme Court questions debate on CEC law
items.summary: On [date], the Supreme Court of India asked whether Parliament had conducted a proper debate before enacting the law that governs the appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and Election Commissioners (ECs). The question was raised in a hearing that focused on the constitutional validity of the legislation. The law, passed by Parliament in 2023, amended the Election Commission Act to formalize the appointment process and clarified that the Chief Justice of India (CJI) would only have an advisory role until the legislature enacts a statute. Earlier, the Supreme Court had ruled that the CJI's input was limited to a 'say' rather than a 'vote.' The current inquiry follows reports that the debate on the bill was brief and lacked substantive discussion. The Court has directed the government to provide records of the parliamentary proceedings and to explain why the debate was deemed sufficient. Depending on the findings, the Court may issue a ruling that could affect future appointments and the independence of the Election Commission. The matter is expected to be revisited in the next session of the Court.
